senses: A type of intaglio printing process, in which an image is engraved onto a rotating copper cylinder.
A style of Japanese softcore; glamour photography.
A general strike, shutdown, or other form of protest used in South Asia in which a substantial portion of the population stays home and does not report to work.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi बंध (bandh, “closure”), from Sanskrit बन्ध (bandha). Doublet of bund (“a type of enclosure”).
examples: A week-long bandh was in progress. People had nothing to do.
Opposition parties said that the bandh was a success. The ruling parties said the opposite. Some saw government insensitivity in the bandh and the beginning of the fight against inflationary trends.

senses: A bitless headpiece of rope or straps, placed on the head of animals such as cattle or horses to lead or tie them.
A rope with a noose, for hanging criminals; the gallows rope.
A halter top.
ety: From Middle English halter, helter, helfter, from Old English hælfter, hælftre (“halter”), from Proto-West Germanic *halftrijā (“harness”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to cut”), equivalent to half- + -ter. Cognate with Scots helter (“halter”), Dutch halfter, halster (“halter”), Low German halfter, helchter, halter (“halter”), German Halfter (“halter, holster”).

senses: Money (either notionally or specifically in dollars or other currencies) earned from the sale of oil, often especially as considered among a national economy's principal revenue streams.
ety: From petro- (prefix meaning ‘petroleum; oil export’) + dollar, possibly modelled after Eurodollar.

senses: A reversioner.
An open passage through a wood; a grassy open or cleared space in a forest.
An everglade.
A bright surface of ice or snow.
ety: From Middle English glade, glode, glede (“a gleam of light, bright space, an open space; an open or cleared space in a forest; a bright patch of sky; a bright surface of snow or ice”), of uncertain origin, perhaps from Old English *glǣd, *glād, related to Old English glæd (“shining, bright”), (compare Old Norse glaðr (“bright”)).

senses: The act of enslaving or the state of being a slave; bondage
examples: I should like to take this opportunity to express my wish for success and victory in our struggle against Communism and enslavement and for freedom and peace.

senses: One who, or that which, displaces.
A master craftsman, often employing apprentices or journeymen.
Synonym of hinny (cross between a stallion and a she-ass)
ety: Blend of horse + jenny, or variant of hinny?

senses: The skills and techniques employed by spies.
A fat substitute (a glyceride of sucrose) that cannot be easily digested and therefore adds no fat, calories, or cholesterol to food products; also used as an industrial lubricant.
examples: What concerns me are celebrity magazines, television with 500 channels, some guy's name on my underwear. Rogaine, Viagra, Olestra.

senses: A proponent of clientelism.
Imprinted with a logo.
examples: You can buy our company's logoed shirts at the gift store.
The standard conductor’s uniform is a conservative affair: a single-breasted navy jacket, two logoed brass buttons, and straight-leg, pleatless pants.
He sipped coffee cut with milk from a paper cup logoed: ’bucks!

senses: Serving to impede (slow down) the action of something
ety: Borrowed from French retardant, equivalent to retard (“to slow down”) + -ant.

senses: A person who advocates such policies.

behaviorism (the theory that a mental state is identical to the disposition or tendency to behave in accordance with the physical causes; statements about the mind are reducible to statements of physical behavior)
examples: One criticism sometimes made of behaviourism is that it fails to make a distinction between someone actually being in pain and someone pretending to be in pain.

On both ways of describing behaviourism, it is agreed that (a) mental states are not inner, categorical states of persons, and (b) what makes psychological claims true are subjects’ behavioural dispositions.

senses: Having jaws.
Having a specified type of jaw.
In a trembling or shaking state
A worker in cordwain leather.
A leather from Córdoba.
A member of the Worshipful Company of Cordwainers, a livery company.
ety: From Middle English cordewainer, cordewaner, from Anglo-Norman cordewaner, from Old French cordoan (“(leather) of Cordova”). See also cordovan, itself borrowed from Spanish Córdoba.
examples: For quotations using this term, see Citations:cordwainer.

senses: The act of stopping up, or closing, an opening.
ety: From Latin obtūrātiō. Compare French obturation.

senses: Able to be detected.
examples: The other crucial finding of the report was that there was a detectible “optimism bias” among Google employees.

senses: A fruit tree trained on a low stem, the branches closely pruned.
One who plays the bagpipes.
spherical, shaped like a coccus
A bagworm moth, any member of the family Psychidae.
A Fall webworm (Hyphantria cunea, family Erebidae).
Any North or Central American fish of the family Lepisosteidae.
ety: From Middle English garfysche (“garfish”, literally “spear-fish”), from gor (“spear”) + fisch (“fish”). Cognate with Scots gairfish (“garfish”).

senses: An organism whose genome has been genetically modified.
Synonym of dalesman.
A traditional small Spanish unit of length, equivalent to about 0.16 mm.
ety: From Latin punctum (“point”) via Italian and Spanish punto, from pungō (“to prick, to puncture”). Doublet of point, pointe, ponto, puncto, punctum, and punt.

senses: The fact of something being lethal; the ability of something to kill.
Used to evoke spiritual unity and interpersonal harmony, with varying degrees of sincerity or sarcasm, as referring to the folk song.
ety: From Gullah. Apparently a corruption of the English phrase “come by here” in a spiritual song.

senses: Of or having the characteristics of prokaryotes, especially bacteria.
Of cells, lacking a nucleus.
A stripe or mark; a ridge; a wale.
ety: From Middle English whelke, from Old English hwelca (“pustule, swelling”).

senses: Spanish or Latin American ice cream.
examples: Soul food, African crafts, and helado sellers line the service streets on either side of the parkway, and traffic halts on all side streets to let the masses promenade.
A medium cup of helado at Pampas Helado Argentina in Aliso Viejo includes two flavors, which can be the chocolate alfajor and banana split.

senses: A person who believes in being prepared to survive and is actively preparing for possible future emergencies and disruptions in local, regional, national, or international social or political order.
examples: But why would survivalists flock to Pinterest, a site that was adopted early-on by people who wanted to share design ideas for home goods? In a way, preppers are actually the ideal user for the site.
But there are also French “survivalists” who – at least until about a decade ago – shared the drawbridge mentality of the Americans stocking up on peanut butter and ammo.

senses: One who crams or stuffs.
A book used for accelerated study in preparation for an examination.
A student who studies hard for an examination.
A teacher who aids such a student.
A school whose speciality is helping students to pass certain examinations.
examples: The pigeon crammers of Paris took mouthfuls of grain and water and spat it into the mouth of a pigeon.

senses: The act of adducing or bringing forward.
ety: Borrowed from Latin adductio, adductionis, from adducō (“to bring to oneself”), from ad + ducō (“to lead”). Compare French adduction. Equivalent to adduct + -ion or adduce + -tion. See adduce.

senses: A culinary device that turns food into a spiral shape, like pasta.
A conical chamber at the breech of the bore in heavy ordnance, especially in mortars.
ety: After Louis-Gabriel de Gomer, the French artillery officer who invented the design. Attested in English since the early nineteenth century.
examples: All iron mortars now in use have gomer chambers and brass ones conical.
